system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2195-05-19 20:27:00 to 2195-05-30 11:53:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for acute decompensated heart failure with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema, with a 7 kg weight gain since his last discharge. He developed transient hypotension likely due to accidental doubling of his home medications, which resolved without intervention. He was treated with intravenous Lasix, later transitioned to oral Lasix 160 mg daily, achieving a discharge weight of 79.9 kg with improved symptoms. His INR dropped to 1.7, prompting bridging with heparin and warfarin dose adjustment to 3 mg daily. Metoprolol was restarted at 12.5 mg daily once blood pressure stabilized. Glyburide was held inpatient with transition to sliding scale insulin; atorvastatin and vitamin D were initiated. He was discharged home with home health services and follow-up in the heart failure clinic, with instructions to monitor weight and maintain anticoagulation.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic heart failure
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Though he had no fever or leukocytosis, the clinical appearance 
of his LLE was concerning for cellulitis so he was started on IV

added Zosyn for gram negative/anaerobe coverage.  Team attempted

and redness did not improve so he was again put on IV 
antibiotics.  He completed a 1 week course of Vanc/Zosyn and by

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ with left lower extremity swelling and pain.

TECHNIQUE:  Doppler ultrasound.

FINDINGS:  There is normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation of the left
common femoral, superficial femoral, popliteal, and calf veins.

IMPRESSION:  No DVT.

RADIOGRAPHS OF THE LEFT TIBIA, FIBULA, AND ANKLE

HISTORY:  Left lower extremity swelling and cellulitis.  Question air.

COMPARISONS:  None.

TECHNIQUE:  Left tibia, fibula, and ankle, five views altogether.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence for fracture, dislocation, or bone
destruction.  Vascular calcifications are present.  There is no evidence for
gas within the soft tissues.  Soft tissues appear swollen about the ankle. 
Slight degenerative changes involve the knee and ankle.  Mild degenerative
irregularities involve the mid foot.  A moderate subcalcaneal bone spur is
noted.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence for bone destruction or gas within soft tissues. 
Vascular calcifications.  Mild degenerative changes.

HISTORY:  ___ male with cellulitis of the left lower extremity, not
improving on IV antibiotics.  Assess for focal abscess or CT evidence of
osteomyelitis.

COMPARISON:  Lower extremity radiographs from ___

TECHNIQUE:  ___ MDCT axial images of the lower extremity were acquired with
intravenous contrast.  Images were displayed with 2.5-mm slice thickness. 
Bone and soft tissue algorithms were reviewed.  Coronal and sagittal
reformations were prepared.

CT OF THE LEFT LOWER EXTREMITY WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  There is extensive
subcutaneous soft tissue edema surrounding the distal left lower extremity to
the level of the ankle and proximal left foot.  There is circumferential edema
and severe skin thickening which is nonspecific in appearance, though
corresponds with the history of cellulitis.  No rim-enhancing fluid collection
is identified within the surrounding soft tissues to suggest abscess
formation.  There is no soft tissue air.  Cortical margins are intact without
osteolysis to suggest osteomyelitis.  

There is no acute fracture or dislocation.  No bone destructive lesion is
identified.  

The popliteal artery, and distal branch vessels inclusive of the anterior
tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal branches demonstrate dense
atherosclerotic calcifications.  Small dystrophic alcifications are seen
within the skin and anterior soft tissues of the left lower extremity.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Moderate-to-severe circumferential skin and subcutaneous edema surrounding
the distal left lower extremity and ankle, findings  consistent with
cellulitis per clinical history.

2.  No rim-enhancing fluid collection to suggest abscess formation.

3.  No CT evidence of osteomyelitis.  If there is ongoing clinical concern,
MRI would be a more sensitive modality for evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand your left leg has been swelling and turning red. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. Two days ago, my leg suddenly got very swollen and painful. It’s red and warm to the touch. I couldn’t walk well. I went to my PCP and he sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had chills one night, but no fever. No nausea or vomiting either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any recent injury or cuts on your foot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. But I did have my toenails cut about two weeks ago. My foot’s felt odd since then—like pins and needles—but I didn’t see any open sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be important. We’ll check for infection. You also mentioned a long car ride recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about 2.5 hours. But no calf pain or shortness of breath, so I didn’t think it was a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve already done an ultrasound to rule that out. It came back negative for a clot. We also took X-rays—no broken bones or gas in the tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the redness and swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on how your leg looks, we think it’s cellulitis—an infection of the skin and soft tissue. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin to cover possible bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your response. We also sent blood and urine cultures to see if we can identify the bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Your labs are mostly stable. White count is normal, which is reassuring. We’re adding another antibiotic called Zosyn because you have diabetes, and it helps cover more types of bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the infection spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not spreading, but we want to make sure we’re aggressive, especially with your medical history. We don’t want it to get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your usual meds—torsemide, glyburide, warfarin. We held metformin for now because of the CT scan with contrast you had. We’ll restart it in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg is still quite red and swollen. We tried switching to oral antibiotics yesterday, but it didn’t improve, so we’re back on IV vancomycin and Zosyn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pills didn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not well enough. IV antibiotics get higher levels into the infection. We’ll keep you on IVs for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably about a week. We’ll reassess daily. We also got your urine culture back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly. It shows Klebsiella in your urine, but at a low level. You’re not having urinary symptoms, so we don’t need to treat it. It’s likely just colonization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria in the blood. That’s good news. Means the infection hasn’t spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My leg still hurts, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re also checking your INR today. It was 2.5 yesterday—within your target range for your mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin for years. Had a stroke once, but MRI didn’t confirm it was from a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history is complex, but we’re monitoring closely. We adjusted your warfarin to 3 mg daily for the last two days to keep your INR stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan yesterday to make sure there’s no abscess or bone infection. Good news—it shows swelling consistent with cellulitis, but no abscess or osteomyelitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. The antibiotics are working. Your leg is starting to look better—less red and warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam continues to improve. Swelling is decreasing. We’ll keep the IV antibiotics for one more day, then switch to oral meds for you to finish at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What antibiotics will I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bactrim and Augmentin—two antibiotics together to make sure we clear the infection completely. You’ll take them twice a day for six days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea or rash. If you get severe diarrhea, call your doctor. Also, finish the full course even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day of IV antibiotics. Your leg looks much better—minimal redness, warmth is gone, swelling is mostly in the ankle now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can actually walk better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll start the oral antibiotics today and plan for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I keep my follow-up with my PCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very important. You’ll see your PCP in a few days so they can check your leg and make sure the infection is fully gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs this morning are stable. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but that’s chronic for you. We’re continuing your iron pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia for years. My ferritin is always low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely due to your warfarin and mechanical valve. We’ll keep you on ferrous sulfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heart and COPD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both are stable. No shortness of breath, lungs are clear. We continued your inhalers and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home with a visiting nurse to check your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your medications as prescribed. Weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take Bactrim and Augmentin twice daily for six days. Finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR is 2.5—perfect for your valve. We’re switching your warfarin to 5 mg daily. You’ll have another INR check tomorrow through the visiting nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure they come.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Also, we added calcium and vitamin D to your list—helps with bone strength, especially since you’re on long-term medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had back pain for years. Maybe that’ll help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep you on oxycodone for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your leg is much improved. Just keep up with the oral antibiotics and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I was worried it might be something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. The key was catching it early and treating aggressively. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re cleared to go home. A nurse will come to check your INR tomorrow. Keep all your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if the leg gets red or swollen again, or if you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, continue your heart and diabetes meds exactly as prescribed. No changes unless your doctor says so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve learned to stick to the routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for cellulitis of the left lower extremity, presenting with sudden-onset swelling, erythema, and pain, likely originating from a minor foot injury after toenail trimming. He was treated with intravenous vancomycin and Zosyn due to inadequate response to initial oral therapy. Imaging ruled out DVT, abscess, and osteomyelitis. Blood cultures were negative, and urine culture showed asymptomatic Klebsiella colonization. His infection improved significantly over 11 days, and he was discharged on a 6-day course of oral Bactrim and Augmentin. His chronic conditions, including diastolic heart failure, diabetes, mechanical aortic valve on anticoagulation, and COPD, remained stable. Warfarin was adjusted to 5 mg daily with an INR of 2.5 at discharge. He was instructed to follow up with his PCP and continue all home medications.
